newsitem.title: USA: Japan, U.S. still far apart on insurance.
newsitem.headline: Japan, U.S. still far apart on insurance.

text.p: Japan and the United States remain far apart in their dispute over opening up Japan's $382 billion insurance market, and an agreement is unlikely ahead of elections in both countries, a Ministry of Finance (MOF) official said on Monday.
Japanese Finance Minister Wataru Kubo met with U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky for an informal dinner on Sunday to exchange views on how to proceed with bilateral insurance talks.
The meeting was not designed to be a negotiation, and a date for the next negotiations was not set, he said.

Both Japan and the United States face elections in the next two months. Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto called for general elections on October 20, while U.S. President Bill Clinton faces presidential elections on November 5.

But Kubo, who is in Washington to attend the regular meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank as well as the Group of Seven industrialised nations, agreed with Barshefsky to settle the matter quickly, the official said.
The dispute centres on the implementation of a 1994 bilateral pact.

Washington has accused Tokyo of reneging on the agreement by moving to deregulate its so-called "third sector" niche market, which includes personal accident and health care insurance in which foreign firms already have a strong foothold, before opening its primary life and casualty markets.

In an effort to break the impasse, Japan told the United States last week that Japan may limit domestic insurance subsidiaries from handling some products in the third sector market until January 1, 1997, the official said.

Japan gave permission to domestic life and non-life insurers to establish subsidiaries in each other's sector from October 1, but said it would set conditions on their operations on Monday. The conditions are to be unveiled by the MOF at 0700 GMT.

In Tokyo, insurance industry sources said the MOF was considering a set of deregulatory measures for the country's non-life insurance sector, such as lifting a ban on mail-order sales on auto insurance policies.

This is widely seen by industry sources as another move by Japan to reach a quick solution to the dispute. The United States has said it would take "appropriate action" if Japan does not uphold the 1994 bilateral agreement.
The official said Kubo and Barshefsky discussed conditions to be put on Japanese insurance subsidiaries, but declined to comment on the details and whether the United States was satisfied with them.
Japan and the United States have already failed to meet a self-imposed July 31 deadline for resolving the insurance dispute, and working-level talks earlier this month left the two sides far apart.

Clinton, in a meeting with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in New York last week, urged mutual efforts to resolve the dispute over implementation of the 1994 pact, as well as a dispute over aviation.
